paper_title: InstantFusion: A Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion/flow models have emerged as the de facto paradigms for image generation, giving rise to a diverse family of modern generators with increasingly heterogeneous architectures and representations. Despite their remarkable generation capabilities, the cross-model alignment of latent representations and the consistency of their underlying denoising dynamics remain underexplored. In this work, we uncover an intriguing cross-model compatibility: independently trained generators exhibit similar latent spatial organization, while directly handing off intermediate states between unaligned models can still preserve coarse visual content. Motivated by these observations, we propose InstantFusion, a lightweight shared latent interface that connects the denoising trajectories of heterogeneous image generators. Specifically, to enable flexible cross-model state translation, model-specific Latent AutoEncoders (LAEs) are introduced to project intermediate states from different generators into a shared latent space and decode them into the latent space of a target generator. This shared space is constrained by two complementary objectives: aligning intermediate states derived from the same image at matched noise levels and synchronizing their corresponding local denoising velocities. Once trained, InstantFusion allows denoising to seamlessly transition across frozen generators without requiring a dedicated mapping for every model pair. The versatility of InstantFusion is demonstrated across acceleration, multi-preference composition, cross-architecture on-policy distillation, and cross-model composition, achieving competitive performance across these diverse settings.

Despite their remarkable generation capabilities, the cross-model alignment of latent representations and the consistency of their underlying denoising dynamics remain underexplored. In this work, we uncover an intriguing cross-model compatibility: independently trained generators exhibit similar latent spatial organization, while directly handing off intermediate states between unaligned models can still preserve coarse visual content. Motivated by these observations, we propose InstantFusion, lightweight shared latent interface that connects the denoising trajectories of heterogeneous image generators. Specifically, to enable flexible cross-model state translation, model-specific Latent AutoEncoders (LAEs) are introduced to project intermediate states from different generators into shared latent space and decode them into the latent space of target generator. This shared space is constrained by two complementary objectives: aligning intermediate states derived from the same image at matched noise levels and synchronizing their corresponding local denoising velocities. Once trained, InstantFusion allows denoising to seamlessly transition across frozen generators without requiring dedicated mapping for every model pair. The versatility of InstantFusion is demonstrated across acceleration, multi-preference composition, cross-architecture on-policy distillation, and cross-model composition, achieving competitive performance across these diverse settings. 1. Introduction Diffusion and flow models have emerged as the dominant paradigms for modern image generation [9, 14, 19, 32 34], enabling increasingly powerful generators with diverse architectural designs. Meanwhile, the model landscape has grown substantially more heterogeneous: generative models differ fundamentally in latent representations and conditioning mechanisms [9, 34], network architectures and parameter scales [4, 6, 28], and training or distillation recipes [23, 31, 32, 37]. Despite these structural differences, generative models ultimately learn to map noise onto closely related natural-image distributions under textual conditioning. However, they are typically studied and deployed as isolated systems. This isolation leaves it largely unexplored whether their latent representations admit meaningful cross-model alignment and whether their underlying generative dynamics remain compatible across distinct models. In this work, we observe two indications of compatibility among independently trained generators: First, despite differences in latent dimensionality, tokenization, and parameterization, their intermediate states often exhibit closely related spatial organization (Fig. 2(a)). Second, directly handing an intermediate denoising state from one model to another, without any learned alignment, typically introduces artifacts but can preserve the main subject and coarse spatial layout of the generated image (Fig. 2(b)). These observations suggest that heterogeneous generators may encode partially shared visual structure and that their denoising processes are not entirely disconnected. This naturally raises more practical question: can such partial compatibility be turned into reusable interface for transferring both latent states and denoising dynamics across heterogeneous latent spaces? * Equal contribution. Corresponding author: Yuhang Zang (zangyuhang@pjlab.org.cn). Code is available at https://github.com/InternLM/InstantFusion. InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 1: Overview of InstantFusion. During training, model-specific LAEs map the intermediate states of frozen generators into shared representation space, where both latent states and denoising dynamics are aligned. During inference, sender state is translated through the shared space into the receivers latent space, and an adaptive criterion determines when the receiver takes over denoising. Existing approaches provide only partial answers to this question. Cross-model latent alignment methods establish connections between individual states from different models [2, 3, 24], but they primarily focus on model-pair-specific mappings, lacking both shared representation space that can accommodate multiple generators and an explicit treatment of denoising dynamics. Meanwhile, trajectory stitching methods allow various denoisers to take over at different stages of sampling, but generally assume that the participating models operate within the same latent space [27]. Therefore, transferring denoising trajectories among generators with heterogeneous latent spaces remains an open problem. Motivated by the analysis above, we introduce InstantFusion, lightweight shared latent interface that connects the denoising trajectories of heterogeneous image generators  (Fig. 1)  . Each frozen generator uses model-specific Latent AutoEncoder (LAE) that maps its intermediate states into shared representation and reconstructs them in the models native latent space. To learn this interface, we construct paired intermediate states from the same image at matched noise levels and align their encoded representations. Since state correspondence alone is insufficient for reliable trajectory transfer, additional alignment of the projected local denoising velocities is enforced so that translated states follow the receivers denoising trajectory. At inference, sender state is encoded by the senders encoder and decoded by the receivers decoder into the receivers latent space. This design allows new generators to be incorporated through their own LAEs, enabling flexible cross-model transitions without dedicated pairwise mappings. InstantFusion provides two fundamental interface capabilities: faithful reconstruction and cross-model state transfer. The latter directly enables cross-model composition: composing Qwen-Image [34] with SD3 or FLUX improves GenEval-v2 [16] by 13 points and CVTG-2K [8] by 0.180.28 over the corresponding base models. Building on interface-level capabilities, InstantFusion supports three downstream applications shown in Fig. 1: generation acceleration, cross-architecture on-policy distillation, and multi-preference composition. It achieves 1.83.3 generation speedup while maintaining strong perceptual quality, balances multiple specialized preferences with competitive GenEval-v2 and HPSv2 [35] performance, and enables on-policy knowledge transfer from Qwen-Image to the architecturally distinct SD3. Experiments demonstrate that InstantFusion serves as general interface for capability transfer and composition across heterogeneous image generators. 2 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 2: Cross-model compatibility. (a) Intermediate states from Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1 exhibit similar spatial self-similarity patterns. (b) Direct handoff between related models preserves generation quality, while cross-family handoff retains the main subject and coarse layout. (c) These observations motivate lightweight interface for connecting heterogeneous generators. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Empirical evidence reveals partial compatibility among independently trained image generators, reflected in similar latent spatial organization and the preservation of coarse visual content under direct, zero-shot unaligned handoffs. (2) InstantFusion provides lightweight shared latent interface that aligns intermediate representations and local denoising dynamics, enabling seamless denoising trajectory transfer across heterogeneous latent spaces without pair-specific mappings. (3) We demonstrate InstantFusion across generation acceleration, multi-preference composition, cross-architecture on-policy distillation, showing its potential as general interface for capability transfer among heterogeneous generators. 2. Related Work We discuss key studies here and defer others to the appendix C. Text-to-Image Diffusion Models. Diffusion and flow-based models have become the prevailing frameworks for text-to-image generation [14, 19]. Modern systems commonly perform denoising in learned latent spaces, combining pretrained autoencoders with text-conditioned denoisers [28, 30]. Within this general framework, model designs have become increasingly diverse. Recent generators, including SD3, FLUX.1, Qwen-Image, and Z-Image, differ substantially in their latent parameterizations, denoising architectures, and training objectives [4, 6, 9, 34]. Yet these independently developed generators are typically studied in isolation, leaving the relationships among their intermediate representations and denoising dynamics largely unexplored. Cross-Model Latent Alignment. related line of work investigates whether independently trained generative models develop structurally compatible latent representations. These studies establish cross-model correspondences through linear mappings, relative representations, or closed-form transformations [2, 3, 24, 25]. More recently, learned bridges have been proposed to connect incompatible teacher and student VAE latent spaces, enabling cross-space diffusion distillation [26]. Nevertheless, these approaches operate primarily on isolated latent states and do not model how corresponding states evolve along denoising trajectories. It therefore remains unclear whether static latent correspondence also implies compatibility between the underlying generative dynamics. 3. Methods InstantFusion enables handoff between frozen image generators by aligning their latent representations and denoising dynamics. In Sec. 3.2, we identify spatial self-similarity and preserved coarse semantics across unaligned models. Building on this, Sec. 3.3 equips each generator with model-specific LAE to align and reconstruct intermediate states, while Sec. 3.4 synchronizes dynamic velocities to harmonize trajectories. For inference, Sec. 3.5 introduces an adaptive strategy tracking predicted clean latents for optimal switching. Fig. 1 provides an overview of our full pipeline. 3.1. Preliminaries Flow Matching. Observation: Shared Structure Across Models We identify two concrete signals of latent compatibility across independently trained generators. First, intermediate representations maintain equivalent spatial dimensions across model architectures, such as Qwen-Image ([1, 16, 1, 128, 128]) alongside SD3 and FLUX.1 ([1, 16, 128, 128]), yielding similar spatial patterns that reflect comparable information density (Fig. 2(a)). Second, halting SD3 partway through denoising and handing off the intermediate state to SD3.5 or FLUX.1 to complete the remaining steps produces contrasting outcomes: while same-family handoff yields seamless image, cross-family handoff introduces local artifacts yet clearly preserves the central cup and its coarse layout (Fig. 2(b)). These artifacts confirm that native latent spaces cannot be directly interchanged, whereas the preserved cup layout suggests that some coarse semantic structure is shared across the latent spaces. These insights directly motivate an interface that aligns and reconstructs intermediate states before harmonizing their denoising dynamics. 3.3. (14) The experiments are conducted on four representative text-to-image generators: SD3 [9], Z-Image [6], FLUX.1 [4], and Qwen-Image (Qwen) [34], covering diverse architectures and latent parameterizations. We use 50,000 image-text pairs from the VisPrompt dataset [36] for training, while keeping all generator backbones frozen to optimize only the LAEs. Specifically, the LAEs are parameterized with 32 shared channels, 64 hidden channels, and 128-dimensional 𝜎 embedding, trained with an initial learning rate of 104. The reconstruction, alignment, dynamics-alignment, and norm regularization losses are balanced with weights of 1.0, 1.0, 0.1, and 104, respectively. Further implementation details are provided in the appendix B. As demonstrated in Fig. 5, all training objectives decrease steadily throughout optimization, confirming that the LAEs achieve accurate reconstruction while effectively aligning cross-model latent states and their corresponding denoising dynamics. 4.2. Applications of LAE Generation Acceleration. Tab. 3 shows that InstantFusion accelerates Qwen-Image by combining it with efficient generators. Pairing Qwen-Image with Z-Image-Turbo or FLUX.2-Klein reduces inference time from 18.84s to 4.373s and 2.545s, while achieving GenEval-v2 scores of 33.34, 27.19 and OneIG-Bench averages of 0.5386, 0.5467, without the quality collapse observed in T-Stitch [27]. InstantFusion is further compatible with existing acceleration methods: applying DiCache [5] to InstantFusion reduces latency from 10.64s to 5.70s, while GenEval-v2 changes only from 32.70 to 32.46 and the OneIG-Bench average marginally increases. Cross-Architecture On-Policy Distillation. We leverage InstantFusion for cross-architecture on-policy distillation (OPD), transferring generative priors from stronger teacher (Qwen-Image) to student (SD3) [10, 12, 15, 18, 38]. As shown in Fig. 1(b), InstantFusion projects intermediate states from both models into the shared latent space, enabling the teacher to compute velocity targets directly along the students trajectory. Consequently, Tab. 1b shows that cross-model OPD improves SD3 from 26.27 to 26.46 in HPSv2, with qualitative evolutions illustrated in Fig. 8. Multi-Preference Composition. Tab. 4 evaluates the composition of independently trained reward experts [17, 29]. When combining experts optimized for GenEval-v2 and HPSv2, InstantFusion achieves scores of 30.97 and 30.68, outperforming velocity fusion and closely matching jointly trained multi-reward GRPO. This result shows that InstantFusion can combine existing single-reward experts without the additional optimization required by joint multi-reward training. We observe the same trend when composing HPSv2 and HPSv3 experts, indicating that the shared latent space preserves the respective preferences learned by the individual experts. 4.4. Ablation and Analysis Ablation of Training Objectives. The three objectives serve complementary functions: ℒalign enables crossmodel state translation, ℒrec preserves information fidelity for accurate reconstruction, and ℒdyn aligns denoising trajectories across architectures (Tab. 5). As shown in Fig. ??, omitting ℒdyn causes training divergence during cross-architecture OPD, even with aligned latent spaces. Conversely, removing ℒrec allows cross-model translation but significantly impairs reconstruction quality. These distinct failure modes demonstrate that all 9 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 8: Evolution of generated images over training steps during cross-model OPD. Figure 9: Comparison between the predicted clean images at adaptively selected handoff steps and the corresponding fully denoised outputs, demonstrating preservation of global structure. three loss terms are essential. Adaptive Handoff Analysis. To verify whether the adaptive criterion selects suitable transition step, we compare the clean image predicted at the selected handoff step with the final generated image. As shown in Fig. 9, this early prediction already preserves the coarse spatial layout of the final output. Crucially, this structural consistency indicates that the selected handoff often occurs after the global structure has largely stabilized. LAE Architecture Design. We conduct an ablation to validate the effectiveness of our time-conditioned residual blocks in LAE. Replacing these time-conditioned blocks with standard convolutional layers leads to substantial drop in cross-model handoff performance (Tab. 6), reducing GenEval-v2 by 7.20 when combining Qwen-Image with SD3 and by 19.17 with FLUX.1. This performance gap under an identical layer highlights the representational efficiency of our design. 4.5. Ablation on Three-Stage Rollout Scheduling To verify whether the shared latent interface remains stable under multi-stage model cascading, we evaluate all six permutation schedules among SD3, FLUX.1, and Qwen-Image across three-stage generation pipeline (Tab. 7). Across GenEval-v2 and HPSv2 metrics, the generation quality remains highly consistent regardless of the specific model execution order. 10 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Table 7: Robustness of the shared latent interface across multi-stage rollout schedules. We evaluate different execution orders across three heterogeneous generators (SD3, FLUX.1, and Qwen-Image). The consistent performance across arbitrary transition permutations confirms the stability and invariance of the joint shared latent space under cascading cross-model transfers.

Inference Efficiency Analysis To determine whether the shared latent interface introduces measurable inference overhead, we compare the end-to-end latency of individual generators and LAE-enabled hybrid generation. Two-model hybrids allocate the steps evenly, while the three-model hybrid uses 17/17/16 allocation. After three warm-up runs, each configuration is measured over 20 runs, with the results reported in Table 8. Since each handoff only translates the latent state without invoking an additional denoiser evaluation, InstantFusion introduces no extra theoretical NFE. 5. Limitations While InstantFusion provides lightweight interface for cross-architecture state and dynamics translation without pair-specific mappings, several limitations remain. Currently, our formulation relies on shared autoencoder and compatible time parameterization across generators. Furthermore, executing hybrid inference requires hosting multiple frozen backbones simultaneously, incurring elevated memory and storage overhead. Extending this interface across heterogeneous autoencoders and optimizing dynamic model loading/offloading represent key directions for future research. 6. Conclusion In this work, we introduced InstantFusion, shared latent interface that connects heterogeneous image generators by aligning their latent states. Without modifying the frozen generators, InstantFusion enables cross-model state transfer. Results across diverse range of downstream tasks further demonstrate the flexibility and broad applicability of InstantFusion. Future work may develop the learned shared space into reusable pretrained interface, such that new generators can be incorporated with minimal adaptation and benefit from common starting point for model composition, knowledge transfer, and downstream optimization. 11 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators

Appendix The supplementary material is organized as follows. Sec. provides implementation and training details for the shared latent interface and cross-model OPD; Sec. reviews additional related work; Sec. reports extended quantitative results, including additional benchmarks, efficiency analysis, and rollout scheduling ablations; Sec. presents additional qualitative examples and handoffs at different denoising steps; and Sec. 5 discusses the limitations of our method. B. Training details Tables 9 and 10 summarize the training configurations. The first stage optimizes only the model-specific LAEs, while cross-model OPD freezes the teacher, reference model, and latent interface and updates only the student LoRA. Additional Related Work Efficient Generation. Existing acceleration methods reduce either the number or the computational cost of denoising evaluations. Few-step methods compress long denoising trajectories into one or few evaluations through distillation or consistency learning [23, 31, 32, 37], while caching-based methods reduce per-step computation by reusing or forecasting intermediate features across adjacent timesteps [5, 21, 22]. Model scheduling methods such as OMS-DPM and T-Stitch further assign different pretrained models to different denoising stages [20, 27]. These studies demonstrate the potential of multi-model acceleration, but have primarily considered models whose intermediate states are directly interchangeable. Composing independently developed generators with heterogeneous latent spaces remains largely unexplored. Diffusion On-Policy Distillation. On-policy distillation (OPD) has proven effective in large language models [1, 13]. Its extensions to diffusion and flow models follow two main directions: on-policy self-distillation uses privileged information to construct stronger teacher from the student itself [15], while teacher-based OPD transfers denoising capabilities from stronger pretrained models along student trajectories [10, 18, 38]. Most methods, however, either assume that teacher and student belong to the same model family or bridge heterogeneous models by comparing their decoded outputs in frozen visual representation [11, 12]. How to directly transfer teachers denoising dynamics to student with an incompatible latent space therefore remains an open question. InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 10: Cross-model state handoffs at different denoising timesteps (Qwen-Image, Flux.1). Multi-Preference Composition. Multi-preference generation is commonly formulated as learning single model that balances several objectives. Prior methods either jointly optimize one generator with multiple reward signals or separately fine-tune preference-specific models and merge their parameters [17, 29]. The former encodes preference trade-offs through multi-objective training, whereas the latter relies on compatible architectures and weight-space interpolation. In both cases, preference composition remains tied to model training or parameter manipulation, limiting the flexible reuse of independently trained experts. D. Per-Model Reconstruction Analysis Beyond Average Metrics While Table 1a summarizes the average reconstruction fidelity across generators, Table 11 provides granular per-model breakdownreporting PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across 1, 5, and 10 latent round trips. This detailed evaluation highlights how reconstruction errors accumulate over sequential cross-model translations, confirming the stability limits of the shared latent space. E. Extended Qualitative Results E.1. Handoffs at Different Denoising Steps To evaluate the trajectory-wide alignment of the proposed LAE across the generation process, we conduct cross-model handoffs at arbitrary intermediate timesteps. As depicted in Figs. 10 and 11, transitions between source and target generators execute reliably at virtually any stage of denoising. This flexibility confirms that our LAE maintains robust state and dynamics alignment throughout the entire trajectory, rather than being restricted to specific timestep windows. 16 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 11: Cross-model state handoffs at different denoising timesteps (Qwen-Image, SD3). E.2. Additional Results across Applications To further evaluate the versatility and qualitative fidelity of InstantFusion, this section provides extended visual comparisons across diverse downstream configurations. Specifically, Figs. 12, 13, and 14 depict singletrip and multi-trip latent reconstructions across SD3, FLUX.1, and Qwen-Image, verifying that our shared representation consistently preserves spatial structures across distinct autoencoder designs. Next, Figs. 15 and 16 showcase cross-architecture handoffs from Qwen-Image into SD3 and FLUX.1 respectively, highlighting robust state migration between heterogeneous model families. Fig. 17 illustrates the synergistic acceleration. Finally, Figs. 18 and 19 demonstrate multi-preference composition results across distinct reward alignmentscombining instruction adherence (GenEval-v2) with aesthetic preference (HPSv2), and coupling multi-domain aesthetic metrics (HPSv2 and HPSv3), respectively. 17 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Figure 12: Qualitative comparison of shared latent reconstruction (SD3). 18 InstantFusion: Shared Latent Interface for Heterogeneous Image Generators Table 11: Reconstruction fidelity under different shared-space configurations.
